claims.text: Multiple principal elements produce severe intrinsic lattice distortion in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Intrinsic lattice distortion slows atomic diffusion.
Lattice distortion combined with irradiation-induced ballistic mixing impedes defect clustering.
Lattice distortion combined with ballistic mixing impedes elemental segregation.
The proposed synergy maintains a fine nanocrystalline structure under extreme conditions.
The proposed synergy maintains a chemically homogeneous, single-phase structure under extreme conditions.
A sputtered W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf nanoalloy can have an initial grain size of approximately 20–30 nm.
The initial W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf film is a homogeneous, single-phase BCC alloy.
Annealing W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf at 1173 K for 30 minutes produces only minimal grain growth.
A W-Ta-V-Cr high-entropy alloy suppresses observable irradiation-created dislocation loops under high-temperature irradiation.
Nanograin boundaries and lattice-distortion-derived dislocations act as defect-recombination centers.
Ballistic mixing reinforces the defect-recombination function of grain boundaries and intrinsic defects.
Slower diffusion reduces the thermodynamic drive for grain growth and precipitation.
Ballistic mixing continuously redistributes atoms and thereby prevents local elemental clustering.
After identical treatment, a lower-entropy quaternary control will show more grain growth than the quinary alloy.
After identical treatment, a lower-entropy quaternary control will show more segregation and precipitation than the quinary alloy.
The stabilization prediction applies up to approximately 1173 K for about 30 minutes.
Longer exposures or substantially higher temperatures will overcome the proposed kinetic barriers and cause microstructural evolution.

contradictions.description: The mechanism depends partly on ballistic mixing, but the specified controlled falsification experiment uses thermal annealing alone. That comparison does not activate or independently vary irradiation-induced ballistic mixing and therefore cannot distinguish the claimed synergy from ordinary thermal-diffusion or composition effects.
